recommendations.reason: See another Ohio material pass through many hands
Follow glass from workshop to gallery
Look closer at a familiar Ohio-made material

blocks.text: Ooh, look at this little whistle. A sheet of brass becomes something you can hold in one hand—and hear across a playground. Let’s start with the flat metal and follow the work that gives it a voice.

Take a metal whistle from a desk drawer and turn it over. Its sound seems to come from one tiny opening, but the object began as several carefully shaped pieces. American Whistle Corporation says it has made metal whistles in Columbus since 1956. Its published process starts with brass sheet or coil, then moves through cutting, forming, joining, and a final sound check.

blocks.title: From brass stock to finished whistle

steps.title: Cut
steps.text: A press cuts flat blanks for the body and mouthpiece from brass stock.

steps.title: Form
steps.text: Tools bend the blanks into the curved shapes the whistle needs.

steps.title: Fit
steps.text: The mouthpiece and body are joined around the air passage, with a small pea set inside the chamber.

steps.title: Listen
steps.text: The company says finished whistles are tested by hand for sound.

blocks.caption: A pea whistle in section. Air passes through the mouthpiece; the moving pea changes its sound into a trill. Simplified, not to scale.

blocks.text: See the little pea inside? It moves around and interrupts the airflow, giving the whistle its trill. Such a small piece, and you can hear the difference.
blocks.title: Listen for the little sphere

blocks.text: That sequence gives us a way to read the object. Start at the mouthpiece and trace the route air would take. Look for the chamber, the opening, the seam, and the ring. Each feature belongs to the sound-making path or to the practical job of carrying and using the whistle. American Whistle’s explanation says the moving sphere interrupts airflow in the chamber, producing the familiar trill. The pea is not decoration; the space around it lets it move.

The first close look is almost a miniature manufacturing diagram: sheet, cut, bend, join, test. The company says it still uses original machinery and produces more than a million whistles a year. Its visit page lists factory tours; check current booking and access information before planning around one.

In Cincinnati, another familiar object follows a slower path. Rookwood Pottery dates its beginnings to 1880, when Maria Longworth Nichols Storer established a pottery in a former schoolhouse and potters worked with Ohio River clay. Rookwood says each piece passes through at least thirteen sets of hands. Rookwood says each piece passes through at least thirteen sets of hands.

Clay changes as it is shaped, dried, decorated, glazed, and fired. Each stage narrows the choices available at the next one. A curve that looks effortless on a finished vase has to survive those changes; a glaze is both a surface and the result of a process. Rookwood’s account stresses patience and allows that small variations are part of handmade work. Notice where a form is regular, where a glaze gathers, and where the maker has left a mark.
Designs shall be original, individuality shall be the goal.
blocks.attribution: Maria Longworth Nichols Storer, quoted by Rookwood Pottery

blocks.text: That line points to a tension worth seeing in a workshop: a vessel is a usable thing, but it can also carry an artist’s distinct choices. Rookwood’s history records a gold medal at the Paris Exposition within ten years of its 1880 founding; a Cincinnati Public Library honors list gives the year as 1889. A Cincinnati Art Museum catalog also preserves the record of an 1882 vase.

blocks.title: Follow the material across the state

blocks.text: Now the two objects open onto Ohio’s other material stories. A whistle makes airflow audible; glass makes light and heat part of what we see; rubber turns flexibility and wear into questions about a tire’s contact with the road. The Toledo Museum’s account of its two 1962 glass workshops describes artists experimenting with studio furnaces, a different kind of making history. Akron’s rubber story connects everyday products to industrial research and workers in the rubber shops. The materials follow different paths through Ohio’s workshops and industries.

Try one small comparison. Put a whistle, a glazed cup, a glass vessel, and a tire tread in your mind’s eye. Ask what each material has to withstand, what process changes its shape, and what the finished object lets someone do. Then ask whose work the object makes easy to overlook. Look closely at what each finished object hides: repeated labor, skilled judgement, and the hands that made it.

items.label: In Cincinnati
items.text: Rookwood lists its working facility and showroom at 1920 Race Street. Its scheduled factory tours enter a live factory, require closed-toe shoes, and cover a large area. Confirm current availability and access arrangements directly.
